# Setup 👀

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(effectsize)   # cohens_d(), eta_squared()
library(car)          # leveneTest()
```

```{r}
#| label: fmt
#| include: false

# numbers in the text: fixed decimals, typographic minus
fmt <- function(x, d = 0) sub("-", "−", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pfmt <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data

leadership    <- read.csv("data/leadership_study_between.csv")
communication <- read.csv("data/communication_study.csv")
ab_test       <- read.csv("data/exercise_data.csv")
```

---

# Part 1: Comparing two groups

## 1.1 Does leadership training improve team performance? 👀

```{r}
#| label: leadership-plot

ggplot(leadership, aes(x = group, y = team_performance)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "red")
```

```{r}
#| label: leadership-assumptions
#| warning: false

leadership |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(team_performance)$p.value)

lev_l <- leveneTest(team_performance ~ factor(group), data = leadership)
lev_l
```

Both Shapiro–Wilk p-values and Levene's p-value
(`r fmt(lev_l[1, "Pr(>F)"], 3)`) are above 0.05: no sign against normality
within the groups or against equal variances. The classic t-test is fine.

```{r}
#| label: leadership-test

t_l <- t.test(team_performance ~ group, data = leadership, var.equal = TRUE)
t_l
d_l <- cohens_d(team_performance ~ group, data = leadership)
d_l
```

- The training group scores `r fmt(diff(t_l$estimate), 1)` points higher
  on average (p `r pfmt(t_l$p.value)`).
- Cohen's d = `r fmt(abs(d_l$Cohens_d), 2)`: a large effect. The sign of
  `cohens_d()` only reflects the order of the groups (control − training).

## 1.2 Your turn ✍️ — the A/B test

**a.**

```{r}
#| label: ab-plot

ggplot(ab_test, aes(x = design, y = time_on_site)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "red")
```

**b.**

```{r}
#| label: ab-levene

lev_ab <- leveneTest(time_on_site ~ factor(design), data = ab_test)
lev_ab
```

Levene's p-value is `r fmt(lev_ab[1, "Pr(>F)"], 3)` — below 0.05: the
variances differ (the boxes have different heights). So: Welch's t-test.

**c.**

```{r}
#| label: ab-test

t_ab <- t.test(time_on_site ~ design, data = ab_test)
t_ab
d_ab <- cohens_d(time_on_site ~ design, data = ab_test)
d_ab
```

- Mean time: Complex `r fmt(t_ab$estimate[1])` s, Simple
  `r fmt(t_ab$estimate[2])` s — the complex design keeps visitors
  `r fmt(t_ab$estimate[1] - t_ab$estimate[2])` seconds longer (p
  `r pfmt(t_ab$p.value)`).
- Cohen's d = `r fmt(abs(d_ab$Cohens_d), 2)`: a large effect.
- Whether longer is *better* is another question: time on site is not sales.

# Part 2: Comparing three or more groups

## 2.1 Which communication method satisfies most? 👀

```{r}
#| label: comm-plot

ggplot(communication, aes(x = communication_method, y = satisfaction_score)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "red")
```

```{r}
#| label: comm-anova

anova_model <- aov(satisfaction_score ~ communication_method, data = communication)
summary(anova_model)
```

```{r}
#| label: comm-lm

lm_model <- lm(satisfaction_score ~ communication_method, data = communication)
anova(lm_model)
coef(lm_model)
```

- F = `r fmt(summary(anova_model)[[1]][["F value"]][1], 1)`, p
  `r pfmt(summary(anova_model)[[1]][["Pr(>F)"]][1])`: at least one method
  differs from the others — ANOVA does not say which.
- `aov()` and `lm()` give the same F and p-value: ANOVA is a regression with
  a categorical variable.
- Email comes first alphabetically and is the reference group: the intercept
  (`r fmt(coef(lm_model)[[1]], 2)`) is its mean; face-to-face scores
  `r fmt(coef(lm_model)[[2]], 2)` and video calls
  `r fmt(coef(lm_model)[[3]], 2)` points higher.

## 2.2 Your turn ✍️ — effect size, post-hoc tests, reference group

**a.**

```{r}
#| label: comm-eta

eta <- eta_squared(anova_model)
eta
```

η² = `r fmt(eta$Eta2[1], 2)`: the method explains about
`r fmt(100 * eta$Eta2[1])` % of the variance in satisfaction — a large effect
(0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large).

**b.**

```{r}
#| label: comm-tukey

TukeyHSD(anova_model)
```

Face-to-face and video calls both differ significantly from email; they do
not differ from each other (p ≈ 0.97).

**c.**

```{r}
#| label: comm-relevel

communication_f2f <- communication |>
  mutate(communication_method = relevel(factor(communication_method), ref = "face_to_face"))
coef(lm(satisfaction_score ~ communication_method, data = communication_f2f))
```

Same model, other comparisons: email scores
`r fmt(coef(lm_model)[[2]], 2)` points lower than face-to-face.

# Part 3: How many participants do you need?

## 3.1 Power analysis 👀

```{r}
#| label: power-n

power.t.test(delta = 9, sd = 9, power = 0.80)
```

```{r}
#| label: power-power

power.t.test(n = 30, delta = 9, sd = 9)
```

For a large effect (d = 1), 17 per group are enough for 80 % power; with 30
per group, the leadership study had a power of about 97 %.

## 3.2 Your turn ✍️ — a small effect

**a.**

```{r}
#| label: power-small

power.t.test(delta = 0.3, sd = 1, power = 0.80)
```

**b.**

```{r}
#| label: power-small-2

power.t.test(delta = 0.3, sd = 1, power = 0.90)
power.t.test(n = 30, delta = 0.3, sd = 1)
```

For d = 0.3: 176 participants per group for 80 % power, 235 for 90 % — and
with 30 per group, the power is only about 21 %. A study that small would
miss a real small effect four times out of five.

---

# Key takeaways

1. **Look first, then test:** plot the groups, check the assumptions, and
   choose the test accordingly (classic vs Welch).
2. **Report effect sizes**, not only p-values: statistical significance is
   not practical importance.
3. **Plan the sample size** before the experiment: small effects need large
   samples.
